title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑based success rates. The preregistered design (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) specified 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded) evaluated with a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The execution used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks from a deterministic generator and shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and therefore no guarded exclusions or replacements were performed. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts to explain why this run produced a degenerate null (synthetic provenance + shared generation reduced sensitivity), and we provide artifact‑grounded recommendations and reproducibility notes for future contamination audits that aim to detect leakage in web‑sourced benchmarks.

sections.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) are being applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Operational adoption requires that benchmarked performance reflect real capabilities rather than artifacts introduced by dataset contamination (items appearing in model training data) or by low‑complexity templated tasks. Meta‑analyses and recent benchmark studies highlight contamination and construct‑validity risks and recommend contamination‑aware audits and verifier‑backed oracles. We preregistered a narrow confirmatory audit to answer: under conservative deterministic detectors (exact token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change a single hosted LLM's validator pass rate?

Contributions. (1) A complete preregistered confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation revealing why this execution produced a degenerate null outcome and concrete, artifact‑grounded prescriptions to increase sensitivity in future audits. We emphasize scope limits: because the executed sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and shared generation semantics, the observed zero flags and null paired difference apply to this synthetic sampling regime and do not imply absence of contamination in independent web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑for‑NetOps research. Prior system papers and benchmarks show LLMs can produce plausible device configurations or repairs under constrained settings and that adding verifiers or iterative repair loops improves average repair quality (e.g., recent benchmark and system works on configuration repair and intent translation). Formal network verification (Header Space Analysis and localized sub‑specification) and verifier families are practical oracles for reachability and policy correctness and are commonly used in generate–validate workflows.

Evaluation validity and contamination audits. Surveys and framework papers document two recurring evaluation risks: contamination and construct invalidity (templated, low‑complexity tasks). These works motivate contamination detectors (exact matching and fuzzy n‑gram overlap) and conservative guarded policies (exclude high‑confidence flagged items, replace deterministically). Our work implements a preregistered subset of these defenses in a confirmatory design and contributes an artifact‑anchored reconciliation of preregistered intentions vs observed execution evidence. We do not attempt to replace broad benchmark curation; rather, we present a reproducible audit protocol and a concrete record of how execution semantics can nullify intended contrasts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The audit was preregistered (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs, tested with exact McNemar two‑sided test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) as implemented in the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor.

Detectors and guarded policy (preregistered). We preregistered three detectors: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity thresholds at 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to model cutoff metadata. The guarded policy deterministically excluded only high‑confidence flags (exact match OR fuzzy ≥ 0.80) and specified deterministic replacement via retemplating and topology augmentation from the same generator distribution with fixed seeds; replacements required an embedding similarity gate prior to acceptance. These rules and replacement semantics are recorded in the archived transformation manifest.

Sampling, task generation, and critical execution semantics. The preregistration permitted deterministic task generators for reproducibility and allowed shared generation semantics when appropriate. The executed run used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to generate synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for the 150‑item confirmatory sample. Execution set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics): when no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, a single shared model generation per item served both baseline and guarded episodes. This execution choice is recorded in model_configuration.json and task_manifest.jsonl in the archive. Because the single shared generation per item was reused by both conditions when exclusions were absent, the paired contrast relied entirely on whether the detectors triggered exclusions; absent exclusions, the baseline and guarded outputs were identical by design.

Model, validator, and scoring. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (execution configured as a hosted model); verification used deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The validator performs parse→state‑update→property checks and yields a binary pass/fail plus detailed traces (observed_touched_field_count, required_command_count, parsed_command_count, final_state, and violation codes). The scoring rule for intent→configuration tasks was full_intent_constraint_validation: a generated configuration must produce the intended final state and respect workflow constraints.

Planned analyses and sensitivities. The primary confirmatory analysis is the paired test above. Prespecified sensitivities included treating failed model calls as failures, exploring fuzzy thresholds at 0.50/0.65/0.80, and subgrouping by templated vs realistic items. Power guidance in the preregistration explained that the originally intended multi‑model plan would detect ≈5 percentage‑point paired differences at 80% power; the single model/single‑call execution reduces observable sensitivity and increases the minimal detectable effect.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than the preregistered maximum of 300. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 150 and consistent provider call accounting; all deterministic consistency checks passed.

Contamination detector outcomes. The preregistered detectors recorded zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample. The archived contamination_summary artifact contains no flagged episodes. The detector workflow in this execution recorded explicit overlap outputs and replacement operations only when high‑confidence flags triggered replacement handling; because no episodes reached the high‑confidence threshold, the detector logs did not produce a per‑item overlap distribution summary for reporting. This absence of per‑item overlap statistics is an explicit, archived execution fact and therefore we do not report inferred overlap summaries that are not present in the archive.

Validator outcomes and primary estimand. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode validator traces and responses are archived and available in the execution bundle.

Representative exemplar and validator diagnostics. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) shows identical normalized_reference_answer and normalized_response: "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up"; the validator returned score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION) with parsed_command_count = 4 and required_command_count = 4. Representative response and validator_trace files for multiple items are provided in the archive and are referenced by filenames in the execution manifest.

What is (artifact‑groundedly) not observed. The archive documents that no replacement operations occurred and that no per‑item fuzzy‑overlap distribution was recorded because no flags met the preregistered high‑confidence threshold. Therefore the results cannot report the distance of sampled items to the preregistered fuzzy threshold; the archive explicitly lacks such summaries for this execution. The absence is itself an execution outcome and grounds our design recommendations below.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the degenerate null. Two executed facts in the archive explain the degenerate paired result. First, the confirmatory sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (documented by source_identifier entries in the task manifest). Synthetic provenance reduces the chance of exact token matches or high fuzzy n‑gram overlap with public web corpora. Second, the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false): when protected exclusions do not apply, the same single generated candidate is reused for both baseline and guarded episodes for an item. Together these facts produced identical baseline and guarded outputs for every item, making the paired contrast uninformative about generation‑level contamination in this execution.

What the execution does and does not answer. This artifact‑anchored run answers the preregistered methodological question within the executed sampling and generation regime: for provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and the preregistered conservative detectors, do high‑confidence flags occur and do guarded exclusions alter validator pass rates? For this execution the answer is no. The execution does not estimate contamination prevalence in independent public benchmarks nor adjudicate subtler contamination modes (paraphrase leakage) because the sampled items, detector logging policy, and generation semantics limited sensitivity.

Design lessons and concrete recommendations. Drawing on the preregistration and archived execution traces, we recommend audit changes to increase sensitivity to public‑corpus contamination: (1) sample provenance‑rich, web‑sourced items rather than provenance‑stable synthetic tasks to exercise exact‑match and fuzzy overlap detectors; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded conditions use independent generations and cannot collapse to shared outputs; (3) widen model scope to multiple independently seeded LLM instances to detect cross‑model contamination signals; (4) log per‑item fuzzy overlap scores for all items (not only flagged ones) so auditors can report overlap distributions irrespective of thresholded flags; (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and a small manual adjudication pool for borderline scores. Each recommendation follows directly from archived artifacts: the execution manifest, deterministic_reconciliation, and analysis artifacts show the current run's synthetic provenance, shared generation semantics, and empty contamination_summary that motivate the above improvements.

Operational implications for NetOps benchmarking. For practitioners auditing public benchmarks, the audit shows sensitivity depends on sampling provenance, detector granularity, and generation semantics. Verifier‑backed validators are valuable functional oracles, but auditor designs must ensure samples exercise detector capabilities and that detectors record granular outputs. Finally, passing a deterministic validator indicates fulfillment of the validator's checks but does not imply production readiness or absence of regressions outside the oracle's scope.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors on a reproducible 150‑pair synthetic NetOps sample. The run produced zero preregistered high‑confidence flags and identical validator pass rates for baseline and guarded conditions (150/150 each), yielding a paired difference of 0.0 pp (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; McNemar p = 1.0). The archive demonstrates that this null outcome arose from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared_generation semantics rather than evidence that public benchmarks lack contamination. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations—provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model scope, per‑item detector logging, and paraphrase‑sensitive detectors—to increase audit sensitivity in future work. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived in the execution bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement; the archive supports full verification of the claims made here.

Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Key execution facts archived in the bundle: the run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"), and execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) so baseline and guarded episodes reused a single generated candidate per item when no high‑confidence exclusions applied. The preregistered primary estimand, analysis executor, sampling plan, detector rules, and replacement semantics are archived. The exact immutable initial master‑prompt reference is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature search, gap selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI peer review simulation, and revision. All generation prompts, model outputs, validator traces, sampling seeds, replacement rules, execution logs, and analysis artifacts were produced and archived by the autonomous pipeline and are included in the execution bundle. No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or the Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development and rehearsal runs occurred (permitted) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence for this final study unless re‑created under the locked pipeline. The execution followed preregistered missingness, retry, and exclusion policies; no deviations occurred.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini): results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 checks specified functional constraints; passing indicates those constraints were satisfied but does not imply comprehensive production readiness nor the absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
